chapter: Teschemacher, Pee Wee, Noon and Simeon
title: Teschemacher's attack, intonation and Chace's flat playing
summary: Chace loves Teschemacher's cracking attack despite Jacobson's resentment, and they debate his flat intonation, which Chace says he picked up too.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well, Jacobson told me once that he felt a little resentment of Teschmacher because he felt Teschmacher was a little overbearing in his playing. He kind of took over the band. He, I don't know, I don't know if he had particular volume, but he, but that crashing attack that he'd play with evidently riled some of the other members in the orchestras he was working with. They thought he was, he was fighting too hard, he was playing a little too desperately. But for my part, that's what I love. I, I only know the records, naturally. And that's what struck me, that, that cracking attack that he'd play with and, and other characteristics of, of good clarinet playing that we've been discussing in these other fellows. Uh, Tesch simply gave those, those, uh, considerations second place. If his intonation went sour or, or, or he squawked or something went wrong, so what? The, uh, that, that feeling, that he had to get the feeling in there.

Do you think it might have been, uh, just that he hadn't been playing long enough to command the instrument, that is five more years, and Teschmacher might have played with a clean execution, yet using the same, uh, uh, fierce dynamics? Maybe it's possible to play that way.
I strenuously doubt it. I, I don't think you can have everything. Maybe some genius will come along who can, uh,

Well, uh, Teschmacher seemed sometimes to be playing outside of the, uh, elastic limits of the instrument. And now, uh, my, my question was, I mean, might be, uh, rephrased. Would he, uh, realize the elastic limits and, and stay within them? And, or would he, uh, uh, explore the instrument till he found some other way to do, uh, uh,
Well, as, as he grew older, or would have grown older, he might have done that, but I would think that would be a function of growing older, rather than a function of his attitude toward playing.
Or be mellowing rather than, uh, uh, uh, actually performing.
He would have found that he had to continue to get work and, and to comply with the, uh,
As long as we're speculating, that's, uh, more likely.
Well, I, you know, I, I prefer to think that he wouldn't. I, I like him very much the way I hear him play. And his intonation doesn't bother me at all. He can play as flat as he likes for my books.
Well, I wondered if some of those things were, uh, also possibly a fault of his ear.

Bud Jacobson developed his ear, so that that, to the point that that intonation was correct. And this, I think, he leaned on, uh, Teschmacher's lead, and said, uh, we can get an effect by playing flat, or, it doesn't matter if you play flat, but it was on the flat side. It wasn't on the sharp side. The bud would usually err.

I think that's true, and that's a problem that's been bothering me ever since I started to play. I'm afraid that, uh, myself, I have, uh, difficulties. I, I tend to play flat. Now, I don't know, uh, as you suggest, the, the, uh, causes, probable causes for this. It might be deficiency in ear. It might be simply that I was so affected by Teschmacher's and Jacobson's and Bud Freeman's playing, when I was awakening to music, that I, uh, adapted this flat feeling about, about playing. You know, Bud played quite flat in the early, early days playing tenor. But, uh, Freeman.
